questions.question: Which of the following best defines Continuous Security Monitoring (CSM)?
questions.option_a: Running SAST and DAST scans once before deployment
questions.option_b: The ongoing observation and analysis of applications, infrastructure, networks, identities, configurations, and security events to identify threats continuously
questions.option_c: The manual review of source code for vulnerabilities on a quarterly basis
questions.option_d: A one-time audit performed after a security incident has occurred
questions.explanation: CSM is continuous observation and analysis of systems and security events to detect threats, vulnerabilities, and incidents in (near) real time, not a one-time activity.

questions.question: Why does security NOT end when an application is successfully deployed, even if it passed SAST, SCA, DAST, and container scanning?
questions.option_a: Because CI/CD pipelines automatically introduce new vulnerabilities after deployment
questions.option_b: Because pre-deployment testing only finds code and dependency flaws, while production faces runtime threats like stolen credentials, insider threats, and unauthorized logins
questions.option_c: Because compliance regulations prohibit relying on pre-deployment testing
questions.option_d: Because DAST tools cannot scan web applications at all
questions.explanation: Pre-deployment testing cannot predict runtime threats such as credential theft, malware infections, privilege escalation, and insider attacks that occur only in production.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the lecture as a new threat that can occur after deployment?
questions.option_a: Insider threats
questions.option_b: Privilege escalation
questions.option_c: A buffer overflow in the source code introduced during coding
questions.option_d: Attacks against APIs
questions.explanation: A coding-phase buffer overflow would be caught by SAST/testing; post-deployment threats listed are stolen credentials, malware, insider threats, unauthorized logins, privilege escalation, and API attacks.

questions.question: In the DevSecOps view, what happens to findings from the Monitor, Detect, Respond, and Learn & Improve stages?
questions.option_a: They are archived and never reused
questions.option_b: They feed back into development, creating a continuous security feedback loop
questions.option_c: They are sent only to management for annual review
questions.option_d: They automatically roll back the deployment
questions.explanation: Unlike the traditional view where Deploy is the end, DevSecOps loops production findings back into development to drive continuous improvement.

questions.question: Which of the following is a main objective of continuous security monitoring?
questions.option_a: Guaranteeing that zero vulnerabilities exist in production
questions.option_b: Reducing the time attackers remain undetected in the environment
questions.option_c: Replacing the need for incident response planning
questions.option_d: Eliminating the need for SIEM platforms
questions.explanation: Key CSM objectives include early threat detection, real-time alerts, and reducing attacker dwell time; it cannot guarantee zero vulnerabilities.

questions.question: A rapid sequence of failed logins (10:35:21, :23, :25, :27, :29) for the same account most likely indicates:
questions.option_a: A user who forgot their password and is retrying normally
questions.option_b: A brute-force attack against the account
questions.option_c: A misconfigured NTP server causing timestamp errors
questions.option_d: Routine automated backup activity
questions.explanation: One failed login may be normal, but a rapid, repeated sequence of failures is a classic brute-force pattern identified during log analysis.

questions.question: Which set of fields would a typical log entry NOT contain?
questions.option_a: Timestamp, user/account, source IP address
questions.option_b: Event type, resource accessed, success/failure status
questions.option_c: The attacker's real name, home address, and motive
questions.option_d: Action performed and error information
questions.explanation: Logs record observable technical facts (time, user, IP, action, outcome); they do not contain an attacker's identity or motive.

questions.question: Which type of log would record IAM changes, resource creation/deletion, and administrative API calls?
questions.option_a: Application logs
questions.option_b: Operating system logs
questions.option_c: Cloud audit logs
questions.option_d: Container/Kubernetes logs
questions.explanation: Cloud audit logs capture cloud control-plane activity: resource lifecycle events, IAM changes, and administrative actions.

questions.question: An organization wants to detect suspicious processes inside containers and pod events in a cluster. Which log sources are most relevant?
questions.option_a: Network firewall logs and email logs
questions.option_b: Container/Kubernetes logs
questions.option_c: Cloud billing logs
questions.option_d: Print server logs
questions.explanation: Container/Kubernetes logs record container activity, pod events, and Kubernetes API requests — exactly what is needed here.

questions.question: What is log management?
questions.option_a: The process of deleting old logs to save disk space
questions.option_b: The process of collecting, centralizing, storing, protecting, analyzing, and retaining logs from different systems
questions.option_c: Writing application code that produces log messages
questions.option_d: The rotation of passwords stored in logs
questions.explanation: Log management covers the full lifecycle of logs — collection through retention — with centralization being the preferred approach.

questions.question: Why is a centralized log management approach preferable to logs kept on individual systems?
questions.option_a: It eliminates the need to configure logging on each host
questions.option_b: It provides centralized visibility, easier threat detection, event correlation, faster investigation, compliance support, and audit-trail preservation
questions.option_c: It makes logs impossible for attackers to read
questions.option_d: It reduces log volume by deduplication guaranteed by law
questions.explanation: Centralization enables correlation across sources and faster investigation; keeping logs only on individual systems fragments visibility.

questions.question: Why must logs be specifically protected against unauthorized deletion or modification?
questions.option_a: Because modified logs cause applications to crash
questions.option_b: Because attackers may try to remove evidence of their activities, destroying the audit trail
questions.option_c: Because log files consume excessive network bandwidth when altered
questions.option_d: Because regulators require logs to be stored on encrypted paper
questions.explanation: Logs are primary evidence; attackers who delete or tamper with them hide their tracks, so integrity and retention protections are essential.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of centralized log management?
questions.option_a: Event correlation across multiple systems
questions.option_b: Faster incident investigation
questions.option_c: Guaranteed prevention of all attacks
questions.option_d: Compliance and audit-trail support
questions.explanation: Centralized logging supports detection and investigation but cannot guarantee attack prevention; no monitoring control can.

questions.question: What is the correct order of stages in a SIEM pipeline?
questions.option_a: Alert → Collection → Normalization → Correlation
questions.option_b: Collection → Normalization → Correlation & Analysis → Threat Detected → Alert → Security Team
questions.option_c: Normalization → Alert → Collection → Correlation
questions.option_d: Correlation → Collection → Alert → Normalization
questions.explanation: A SIEM collects logs from sources, normalizes them into a common format, correlates and analyzes them, detects threats, and alerts the security team.

questions.question: What is the key value of event correlation in a SIEM, as illustrated by '20 failed logins + successful login + new admin created + sensitive data downloaded'?
questions.option_a: Each event is stored more cheaply when grouped
questions.option_b: Individually harmless events, when combined, reveal a likely account compromise
questions.option_c: Correlation automatically blocks the attacker's IP address
questions.option_d: It reduces false negatives to exactly zero
questions.explanation: Correlation links related events across systems to expose attack patterns that no single log entry would reveal.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example SIEM platform mentioned in the lecture?
questions.option_a: Microsoft Sentinel
questions.option_b: Wireshark
questions.option_c: Nmap
questions.option_d: Burp Suite
questions.explanation: Example SIEM platforms given are Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk, IBM QRadar, and Elastic Security; Wireshark and Nmap are network tools, Burp Suite is a web proxy.

questions.question: In DevSecOps, runtime monitoring repeatedly detects attacks against a particular API endpoint. The best 'shift-right' response is to:
questions.option_a: Ignore it, since the endpoint already passed pre-deployment testing
questions.option_b: Feed the production finding back to developers so the API's security controls can be improved
questions.option_c: Permanently shut down the entire application
questions.option_d: Disable all logging on that endpoint to reduce noise
questions.explanation: 'Shift-right' means using production monitoring feedback to continuously improve code and security controls upstream.

questions.question: What is an intrusion?
questions.option_a: Any authorized login by a legitimate administrator
questions.option_b: Unauthorized or malicious activity that attempts to compromise a system, network, or data
questions.option_c: A hardware failure that causes a server outage
questions.option_d: The scheduled deployment of a security patch
questions.explanation: An intrusion is unauthorized/malicious activity such as port scanning, exploitation, brute-force attempts, or malware communication.

questions.question: The key characteristic that distinguishes an IDS from an IPS is that an IDS:
questions.option_a: Detects and alerts but normally does not automatically block the attack
questions.option_b: Sits in-line and drops all malicious packets
questions.option_c: Only monitors application-layer traffic
questions.option_d: Requires no monitoring rules to function
questions.explanation: An IDS is typically passive — it detects and alerts. An IPS is active/in-line and can block traffic automatically.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an action an IPS may take?
questions.option_a: Dropping malicious packets
questions.option_b: Blocking an IP address
questions.option_c: Guaranteeing the attacker is arrested
questions.option_d: Resetting a connection and generating an alert
questions.explanation: An IPS can drop packets, block IPs/connections, reset connections, and alert — but it cannot guarantee law-enforcement outcomes.

questions.question: An e-commerce site must block SQL-injection packets in real time before they reach the database server. Which solution fits best?
questions.option_a: Passive IDS sending alerts to the SOC
questions.option_b: An in-line IPS that drops malicious packets automatically
questions.option_c: Periodic manual log review once a week
questions.option_d: A SIEM that only stores firewall logs
questions.explanation: Real-time blocking requires an active, in-line IPS; a passive IDS would only alert after the traffic arrives.

questions.question: Using the lecture's analogy, an IDS is best compared to ____ while an IPS is best compared to ____.
questions.option_a: a security guard; a security alarm
questions.option_b: a security alarm; a security guard
questions.option_c: a firewall; a router
questions.option_d: a backup system; a SIEM
questions.explanation: An IDS is like a security alarm (detects and raises alert); an IPS is like a security guard (detects and attempts to stop the intruder).

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts signature-based and anomaly-based detection?
questions.option_a: Signature-based uses behavior baselines; anomaly-based uses known attack patterns
questions.option_b: Signature-based compares activity against known attack patterns and has low false positives for known attacks, but may miss unknown attacks; anomaly-based builds a normal-behavior baseline and can catch unknown attacks, but may produce more false positives
questions.option_c: Signature-based detection cannot identify any attacks
questions.option_d: Anomaly-based detection requires no understanding of normal behavior
questions.explanation: Signature detection is strong for known attacks but blind to novel ones; anomaly detection generalizes to unknown attacks at the cost of more false positives.

questions.question: A company deploys a brand-new, never-before-seen attack against your network. Which detection technique is most likely to flag it?
questions.option_a: Signature-based detection with an updated rule set
questions.option_b: Anomaly-based detection, because the attack deviates from the baseline of normal behavior
questions.option_c: Checking the attack against yesterday's antivirus signatures
questions.option_d: Manual review of last year's firewall logs
questions.explanation: Since no signature exists for a brand-new attack, only anomaly-based detection — which flags deviations from normal behavior — has a chance of catching it.

questions.question: Which is a known limitation of anomaly-based detection?
questions.option_a: It cannot detect any attacks
questions.option_b: It may produce more false positives and requires understanding of normal behavior
questions.option_c: It only works against DDoS attacks
questions.option_d: It is always slower than manual review
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection's weaknesses are higher false-positive rates and the need to accurately model normal behavior.

questions.question: Which of the following is a security EVENT but NOT necessarily a security INCIDENT?
questions.option_a: Ransomware encrypting production databases
questions.option_b: A firewall denying a single connection attempt, which is an observable occurrence that may or may not compromise security
questions.option_c: An attacker exfiltrating customer data
questions.option_d: A compromised container running cryptominers
questions.explanation: A security event is any observable occurrence; only when it actually or potentially compromises security or violates policy does it become an incident.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders the six Incident Response lifecycle phases?
questions.option_a: Detection → Preparation → Containment → Recovery → Eradication → Lessons Learned
questions.option_b: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned
questions.option_c: Containment → Preparation → Detection → Recovery → Eradication → Lessons Learned
questions.option_d: Preparation → Containment → Detection → Eradication → Lessons Learned → Recovery
questions.explanation: The canonical IR lifecycle is: prepare first, then detect/analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, and finally capture lessons learned.

questions.question: During the Preparation phase, an organization should primarily:
questions.option_a: Delete all logs to save storage
questions.option_b: Establish the IR plan, roles, communication procedures, monitoring, backups, and security controls
questions.option_c: Announce the incident to the public
questions.option_d: Rebuild all servers from scratch
questions.explanation: Preparation builds readiness before any incident: plans, roles, playbooks, monitoring, and backups.

questions.question: A host is isolated from the network to stop malware from spreading, but the malware is still on the disk. Which phase is the team in, and what comes next?
questions.option_a: Eradication; next step is containment
questions.option_b: Containment; next step is eradication (removing malware, patching, deleting malicious accounts)
questions.option_c: Recovery; next step is lessons learned
questions.option_d: Detection; next step is preparation
questions.explanation: Isolation is containment (limiting spread); eradication then removes the root cause — malware removal, patching, and deleting malicious accounts.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the Lessons Learned phase?
questions.option_a: To assign blame to individual employees
questions.option_b: To review the incident and improve security so it does not recur
questions.option_c: To restore systems from the most recent backup
questions.option_d: To contain the attacker's lateral movement
questions.explanation: Lessons learned closes the loop by improving plans, controls, and monitoring based on what the incident revealed.

questions.question: Which statement about the Recovery phase is correct?
questions.option_a: Systems are restored from clean backups, reconnected, and monitored for further issues
questions.option_b: All evidence is permanently deleted
questions.option_c: The IR plan is discarded
questions.option_d: The attacker is given read-only access for verification
questions.explanation: Recovery restores normal operations from clean backups, reconnects systems carefully, and watches for signs of reinfection.

questions.question: In an incident response process, what is the primary responsibility of System/Cloud Administrators?
questions.option_a: Writing press releases for the media
questions.option_b: Isolating and restoring infrastructure
questions.option_c: Deciding regulatory fines
questions.option_d: Designing the company logo for incident reports
questions.explanation: Admins isolate compromised infrastructure and restore systems; analysts investigate, developers fix code/pipeline issues, and management makes business decisions.

questions.question: A developer whose code introduced the vulnerability works with security staff during the incident. Which IR role best describes this, and why does DevSecOps improve IR?
questions.option_a: Legal/Compliance; because lawyers write better firewall rules
questions.option_b: Developer/DevOps Engineer; because developers, operations, and security collaborate rather than operating in silos
questions.option_c: Communication team; because they can patch faster
questions.option_d: Management; because executives can reverse-engineer malware
questions.explanation: Developers/DevOps engineers fix application and pipeline issues; DevSecOps improves IR precisely because these groups collaborate.

questions.question: A security incident investigation attempts to determine all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.option_a: How the attacker gained access and which systems/accounts were affected
questions.option_b: What actions the attacker performed and whether data was stolen
questions.option_c: The attacker's favorite programming language and personal hobbies
questions.option_d: Whether the attacker is still present and what vulnerability caused the incident
questions.explanation: Investigation reconstructs how, when, what, and which — not personal preferences unrelated to the attack.

questions.question: Which combination of evidence sources is used to reconstruct an attack into an incident timeline leading to root cause?
questions.option_a: Network data, system evidence, cloud audit records, and application evidence
questions.option_b: Employee attendance records and cafeteria receipts
questions.option_c: Only the contents of the company's public website
questions.option_d: Social media posts from the attacker's account
questions.explanation: Reconstruction combines network data, system evidence, cloud audit records, and application evidence into a timeline and root cause.

questions.question: Digital forensics is best defined as:
questions.option_a: The systematic process of identifying, collecting, preserving, examining, analyzing, and reporting digital evidence related to a security incident
questions.option_b: The automated patching of vulnerable systems
questions.option_c: The encryption of all company databases
questions.option_d: The penetration testing of web applications
questions.explanation: Forensics follows a disciplined evidence lifecycle — identification through reporting — to support investigation and potential legal action.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a possible source of digital evidence listed in the lecture?
questions.option_a: Memory and disk images
questions.option_b: Emails and network captures
questions.option_c: Cloud audit logs and container logs
questions.option_d: Handwritten sticky notes on a monitor
questions.explanation: Listed evidence includes system/application logs, network captures, files, memory, disk images, emails, cloud audit logs, authentication records, and container logs.

questions.question: Place the basic digital forensics process in the correct order:
questions.option_a: Analysis → Identification → Collection → Preservation → Examination → Reporting
questions.option_b: Identification → Collection → Preservation → Examination → Analysis → Reporting
questions.option_c: Reporting → Preservation → Collection → Identification → Analysis → Examination
questions.option_d: Collection → Reporting → Analysis → Identification → Preservation → Examination
questions.explanation: The forensic process flows: identify evidence sources, collect, preserve integrity, examine, analyze, and report findings.

questions.question: What is the chain of custody?
questions.option_a: A hardware device that physically locks server racks
questions.option_b: The documented record showing how digital evidence was collected, handled, transferred, stored, and analyzed
questions.option_c: The network path an attacker used to move between systems
questions.option_d: A list of employees authorized to use the SIEM
questions.explanation: Chain of custody documents every handling step of evidence to demonstrate it was not improperly altered.

questions.question: A chain-of-custody record may contain all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.option_a: Description of evidence, evidence identifier, and date/time collected
questions.option_b: Person who collected it, collection location/source, and storage information
questions.option_c: Transfers between individuals and actions performed on the evidence
questions.option_d: The collector's personal opinion of who the attacker probably is
questions.explanation: Chain of custody records factual handling details; speculation about the attacker's identity is not part of it.

questions.question: Why is the chain of custody especially important when an incident leads to legal or disciplinary action?
questions.option_a: Because without it, evidence cannot be encrypted
questions.option_b: Because without proper evidence handling, it may be difficult to demonstrate the integrity and reliability of the digital evidence
questions.option_c: Because courts require evidence to be stored in the cloud
questions.option_d: Because it guarantees the attacker will be convicted
questions.explanation: Courts demand proof of evidence integrity; a documented chain of custody establishes that evidence was not tampered with.

questions.question: Log analysis shows: 09:01 multiple failed logins → 09:06 successful login from unusual IP → 09:08 privilege changed to Administrator → 09:12 database accessed → 09:15 large data download → 09:18 logout. The best interpretation is:
questions.option_a: A routine administrator performing scheduled maintenance
questions.option_b: A credential attack, account compromise, privilege escalation, database access, and possible data exfiltration
questions.option_c: A failed backup job that should be ignored
questions.option_d: A misconfigured monitoring agent
questions.explanation: Correlated in sequence, these log entries form a complete attack timeline: brute force → compromise → escalation → access → exfiltration.

questions.question: HARD: A SOC analyst sees 500 failed logins from one IP against many different user accounts, then a few successful logins from that IP. Individually each event looks minor. Which capability turns this into a meaningful detection, and on what principle?
questions.option_a: An IDS signature, because each failed login matches a known rule
questions.option_b: SIEM correlation across time and sources, because the combined pattern (password spraying + successful compromise) reveals an attack no single log shows
questions.option_c: Log deletion, because removing noise reveals attacks
questions.option_d: Container scanning, because it detects runtime attacks
questions.explanation: Password spraying distributes failures across accounts to evade per-account lockouts; only cross-source, temporal correlation exposes the coordinated campaign.

questions.question: HARD: During containment of a ransomware outbreak, an administrator is tempted to power off all infected servers immediately and wipe them. What is the primary risk of this approach from an incident response/forensics standpoint?
questions.option_a: It violates the containment phase, which forbids any action
questions.option_b: Powered-off or wiped systems can destroy volatile evidence (memory, running processes, network connections) needed to determine root cause and scope
questions.option_c: It will automatically trigger a second ransomware infection
questions.option_d: It makes the chain of custody stronger
questions.explanation: Eradication and recovery must be preceded by evidence capture; memory and live state are lost on shutdown, undermining investigation and lessons learned.

questions.question: HARD: An attacker uses a compromised legitimate account, stays within normal working hours, and mimics typical admin activity to avoid anomaly detection. Which defense-in-depth combination best addresses this?
questions.option_a: Signature-based IDS alone, since it has the fewest false positives
questions.option_b: Layered monitoring: SIEM correlation of IAM, cloud audit, and application logs plus anomaly detection with tight baselines, so low-and-slow abuse still stands out when events are combined
questions.option_c: Disabling all alerting to reduce noise
questions.option_d: Relying solely on employees reporting suspicious behavior
questions.explanation: Living-off-the-land attacks evade single controls; correlating identity, cloud, and application events exposes subtle patterns that evade isolated baselines.

questions.question: HARD: A startup argues that formal incident response planning is unnecessary because 'our monitoring will catch everything.' Which response best reflects the lecture's concepts?
questions.option_a: They are right; monitoring replaces incident response entirely
questions.option_b: Without an IR plan, organizations respond slowly or inconsistently when incidents occur — monitoring detects, but IR plans, roles, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned handle and learn from the incident
questions.option_c: They should only prepare the recovery phase and ignore the rest
questions.option_d: Incident response is only needed for companies with more than 10,000 employees
questions.explanation: Detection alone is insufficient; the lecture stresses that organizations without IR plans respond slowly or inconsistently during incidents.

questions.question: HARD: After an incident is closed, which feedback actions best align with 'an incident is not fixed and forgotten'?
questions.option_a: Updating secure coding practices, threat models, CI/CD security controls, cloud configuration, container security, IAM policies, monitoring rules, and security tests
questions.option_b: Deleting all logs from the incident to save storage
questions.option_c: Blaming a single employee and changing nothing else
questions.option_d: Disabling monitoring alerts that fired during the incident
questions.explanation: Findings must feed back into code, configs, pipeline controls, IAM, and monitoring to create continuous security improvement.
